library(cowplot)

global_temps <- read_csv(file.path('data', 'nasa_global_temps.csv'))

# 1. Visualizing single variables over time

Use the `global_temps` data frame to explore ways to visualize the change in average global temperatures.

Consider using:

- points
- lines
- areas
- smoothed lines

## Points
```{r}
#| label: global-temps-points
#| fig.height: 5
#| fig.width: 6
ggplot(global_temps, aes(x = year, y = meanTemp)) +
    geom_point(color = 'red4', size = 1) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
    theme_half_open(font_size = 16) +
    labs(x = 'Year', y = 'Temperature anomaly (C)')
```

## Line
```{r}
#| label: global-temps-line
#| fig.height: 5
#| fig.width: 6
library(gganimate)

ggplot(global_temps, aes(x = year, y = meanTemp)) +
    geom_line(color = 'red4', size = 1) +
    # Add a reference line at 0
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
    theme_half_open(font_size = 16) +
    labs(x = 'Year', y = 'Temperature anomaly (C)')
```

## Smoothed line
```{r}
#| label: global-temps-line-smoothed
#| fig.height: 5
#| fig.width: 6
ggplot(global_temps, aes(x = year, y = meanTemp)) +
    geom_point(color = 'grey', size = 1.5, alpha = 0.6) +
    geom_smooth(color = 'red4', size = 1, se = FALSE) +
    # Add a reference line at 0
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
    theme_half_open(font_size = 18) +
    labs(x = 'Year', y = 'Temperature anomaly (C)')
```

## Area
```{r}
#| label: global-temps-area
#| fig.height: 5
#| fig.width: 6
ggplot(global_temps, aes(x = year, y = meanTemp)) +
    geom_area(fill = 'red4', alpha = 0.5) +
    geom_line(color = 'firebrick', size = 1) +
    theme_half_open(font_size = 18) +
    labs(x = 'Year', y = 'Temperature anomaly (C)')
```



# 2. Animation

Use the `global_temps` data frame to animate one of the charts we did in the first exercise on changes in average global temperatures.

## Points
```{r}
#| label: global-temps-points-anim
#| fig.height: 5
#| fig.width: 6
library(gganimate)

global_temps_anim_points <- global_temps %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = meanTemp)) +
  geom_point(color = 'red4', size = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  theme_half_open(font_size = 16) +
  labs(
    x = 'Year',
    y = 'Temperature anomaly (C)'
  ) +
  transition_manual(year, cumulative = TRUE)

animate(
  global_temps_anim_points,
  nframes = 100,
  fps = 20,
  width = 600,
  height = 500,
  units = "px",
  res = 100
)
```

## Line
```{r}
#| label: global-temps-line-anim
#| fig.height: 5
#| fig.width: 6
library(gganimate)

global_temps_anim_plot <- global_temps %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = meanTemp)) +
  geom_line(color = 'red4', size = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  theme_half_open(font_size = 16) +
  labs(
    x = 'Year',
    y = 'Temperature anomaly (C)'
  ) +
  transition_reveal(year)

animate(
  global_temps_anim_plot,
  nframes = 100,
  fps = 20,
  width = 600,
  height = 500,
  units = "px",
  res = 100,
  end_pause = 15
)
```


# 3. Visualizing multiple variables over time

Use the `us_covid` data frame to explore ways to visualize the number of daily cases using:

1. A labeled line chart
2. A stacked area chart
3. A heat map

## Labeled line chart

For this one, try showing just the lines for NY and CA.
I already made the summary data frame to do this.

```{r}
#| label: covid-ca-ny
#| echo: false
#| fig.height: 4
#| fig.width: 12
#| fig.align: 'center'

us_covid_ca_ny <- us_covid %>%
  mutate(cases_daily = cases_daily / 10^3) %>%
  filter(state %in% c("California", "New York"))

# Write code here
```

## Stacked area chart

For this one, try showing NY, CA, and all other states.
I already made the summary data frame to do this.

```{r}
#| label: covid-area
#| fig.height: 4
#| fig.width: 12
#| fig.align: 'center'

us_covid %>%
  mutate(
    state = fct_other(
      state,
      keep = c(
        "California",
        "New York"
      )
    ),
    state = fct_relevel(
      state,
      c(
        "Other",
        "California",
        "New York"
      )
    )
  ) %>%
  group_by(day, state) %>%
  summarise(deaths_daily = sum(deaths_daily))

# Write code here
```
